To keep the gallery compact, each full-size photograph is represented by a small preview image called a thumbnail.
The sentence directly beneath the photograph identifies the students and describes the event, making it the image's caption.
The image's description is read aloud by a screen reader when the photograph cannot be seen, so it is alt text.
When the pointer rests on the unfamiliar icon, a small explanatory label appears beside it as a tooltip.
The underlined words 'View timetable' open another page when selected, so the words act as a hyperlink.
Visitors keep asking the same questions about joining, so the designer groups the common questions and answers in the FAQ section.
To explain who founded the club and what its members hope to achieve, the designer adds an About page.
The school's address, telephone number and message form belong together on the Contact page so visitors can get in touch.
The student publishes dated articles about each stage of her project, with the newest first, using a blog.
Rather than displaying every classroom exercise, the designer selects her strongest finished projects to present in her portfolio.
The quoted comment from a satisfied workshop visitor appears with their name and describes their experience, making it a testimonial.
Visitors enter their email address to receive future club updates, so the boxes and Subscribe button form a newsletter form.
Visitors may choose several interests at once, so the form uses square controls that can be ticked independently, called checkboxes.
Visitors must choose exactly one delivery method from a visible group of circular controls, so the form uses radio buttons.
When visitors type their secret login code, the characters are hidden by dots inside the password field.
The form needs space for a message across several lines, so the designer includes a text area rather than a single-line box.
The pale example address inside the email box disappears when typing begins, so it is placeholder text rather than a permanent label.
The words 'Email address' remain above the box after the visitor starts typing, so they are its field label.
As the file uploads, a horizontal indicator gradually fills from zero to one hundred per cent, acting as a progress bar.
The article list is divided into numbered pages with Next and Previous controls, so the designer has added pagination.
The opening image display rotates through three photographs, with arrows for moving between them, so it is a carousel.
Each question expands to reveal its answer beneath it when selected, so the FAQ uses an accordion to save space.
Selecting 'Overview', 'Prices' or 'Dates' changes the content in the same panel, so these controls work as tabs.
The page is dimmed while a confirmation window appears above it and requires a response, so the window is a modal dialog.
The notice asks visitors whether to allow optional tracking files and provides Accept and Reject buttons, making it a cookie banner.
An old link leads to a message explaining that the requested page cannot be found, so visitors see an error page.
The small school symbol beside the website's name in the browser tab is its favicon, helping visitors recognise the open tab.
To help visitors browse the site's overall structure, the designer creates a sitemap listing its pages in organised groups.
Before choosing colours or photographs, the designer draws a simple plan of boxes showing where content will go, called a wireframe.
The team tests a clickable model of the planned website before the real site is built, so they use a prototype.
The photographs line up in repeated rows and columns, giving the gallery a clear grid that keeps the layout organised.
The designer leaves empty space around the heading instead of adding more pictures, using whitespace to separate it from nearby content.
Dark text against a pale background is easier to distinguish than pale text on white because it has stronger contrast.
The title is largest, section headings are smaller and body text is smallest, creating a clear visual hierarchy for readers.
The designer uses the same chosen set of blue, cream and grey shades throughout the site, keeping its colour palette consistent.
The three-column layout becomes a single column on phones, so the site uses responsive design to suit different screen sizes.
The button changes colour only while the pointer rests on it, so the designer has created a visible hover state.
All paragraph edges begin on the same vertical line, so the designer has improved the text's alignment.
Because the site is designed mainly for younger children, those children are its target audience and should guide the language choices.
The club's recognisable symbol appears beside its name on every page, so the designer has repeated the logo for consistency.
Although the article continues for several screens, the navigation remains attached to the upper edge after visitors scroll past its original position, behaving as a sticky header.
Rather than opening a different page, the 'See prices' control moves the visitor directly to the pricing section further down the current page, using an anchor link.
Because visitors can enter through a detailed article without seeing the home page, the designer adds breadcrumbs showing the article's parent sections and its place in the site.
After selecting 'Photography', visitors see only photography projects while the other categories disappear from the results, showing that the category control acts as a filter.
When visitors choose 'Newest first', every project remains available but the sequence changes according to date, so they have used the sort control.
Instead of loading every article into one continuous list, the site divides results into separate numbered screens and supplies Next and Previous links, using pagination.
Since most visitors need only one answer, each FAQ question opens its own answer immediately underneath, while the other questions remain available in an accordion.
The labels 'Description', 'Dates' and 'Prices' remain visible while selecting one replaces the content of a shared panel, so the product information is organised into tabs.
Before deleting a project, visitors must respond to a confirmation window that prevents interaction with the dimmed page behind it, making this window a modal dialog.
To explain an unfamiliar symbol without adding permanent text beside it, the designer makes a brief label appear when the icon receives hover or focus, using a tooltip.
When a visitor presses Tab, a clear outline moves between links and buttons, revealing which control will respond to the keyboard through a visible focus indicator.
To prevent keyboard users from moving through the same long menu on every visit, the designer adds a skip link that jumps directly to the main content.
Because the photograph communicates information that cannot be understood from the surrounding article alone, the designer provides a meaningful text alternative in its alt text.
The interview's spoken words appear as text timed to the video, together with relevant sound information, so viewers can follow it without hearing through the captions.
Visitors who prefer reading can open a separate written record of the interview from beginning to end, rather than following timed text over the video, using a transcript.
The instruction inside the empty box vanishes as soon as typing begins, so the designer adds a permanent field label above it to identify the required information.
When a visitor enters letters into a field that requires a number, the site identifies the affected box and explains the problem through form validation.
After the form is successfully submitted, a short notice confirms that the message was received and explains the expected response time, acting as a confirmation message.
The Submit button cannot be activated until the required agreement is selected, so its inactive appearance communicates a disabled state rather than a temporary loading process.
While the site retrieves a large gallery, an animated symbol tells visitors that processing is still happening, although no completion percentage is available, serving as a loading indicator.
A newly created portfolio has no projects yet, so the page explains the absence and offers an Add project button as part of its empty state.
Although the content remains the same, its columns rearrange automatically to fit the available screen width without requiring sideways scrolling, demonstrating a responsive layout.
At a chosen screen width, the three-column gallery switches to one column and the navigation changes form, so that width is a design breakpoint.
The designer increases the space outside the card's border so neighbouring cards move farther away, while the content inside the card stays unchanged, adjusting its margin.
Because the paragraph sits too close to the inside edge of its bordered box, the designer increases the box's padding without changing the paragraph's words.
Rather than filling every available gap with decoration, the designer leaves deliberate empty areas around related content, using whitespace to improve separation and reduce crowding.
Although individual photographs have different subjects, their edges follow the same underlying system of rows and columns, giving the page a consistent grid structure.
By varying size, weight and position, the designer makes the booking information noticeable before supporting details, establishing a visual hierarchy that guides the order of attention.
The text size remains unchanged, but replacing pale grey letters with dark blue makes them easier to distinguish from the white background by increasing contrast.
Although the heading explains the workshop, the prominent 'Reserve your place' button turns that information into an explicit invitation to act, functioning as the main call to action.
The page prioritises booking, but a quieter 'View the programme' link offers an alternative for visitors who need more information, serving as a secondary action.
Rather than treating the logo and navigation as the main introduction, the designer uses the large opening image, headline and booking button below them as the hero section.
The copyright details and legal links repeat beneath the main content on every page, so they belong in the footer rather than the opening promotional section.
To keep the article itself uninterrupted, the designer places related links in a separate narrow column running alongside the text, creating a sidebar.
Before selecting photographs or typefaces, the team sketches boxes to agree where the main sections should sit, using a wireframe to discuss structure rather than appearance.
The client needs to approve the proposed colours, fonts and imagery, so the designer presents a detailed static visual design, commonly called a mockup.
Because the team needs to test whether visitors can move from an event listing to a booking screen, it creates a clickable prototype before building the finished site.
Rather than asking only whether the colours look attractive, the designer observes visitors trying to find a timetable without help, carrying out a usability test.
Visitors expect workshop dates under Events, but the current site hides them under About, so the designer revises the grouping and labelling of content within its information architecture.
Although the articles change each week, the logo, colours and typography remain recognisable across every page, maintaining a consistent visual identity for the organisation.
The site replaces formal instructions with friendly, direct sentences while keeping its colours and layout unchanged, so the main revision concerns its tone of voice.
Because several equally bright elements compete for attention, the designer makes one image clearly dominant so the page has an identifiable focal point for the viewer.
When the designer changes an image's width and height in different proportions, faces look stretched, showing that the image's original aspect ratio has not been preserved.
The photographs keep the same visible dimensions, but their files become smaller so they transfer more quickly, showing that the designer has used image compression.
To remove a distracting object near the edge while keeping the subject, the designer cuts away part of the photograph instead of stretching it, using cropping.
Although the main menu contains only the most important sections, a separate page provides an organised collection of links to pages throughout the site, forming a sitemap.
The 'Our team' link opens another page on the same website, rather than sending visitors to a different website, so it is an internal link.
Before visitors send personal details through the contact form, a linked notice explains why the information is collected and how it will be used, providing a privacy notice.
Although the telephone number is optional, the form refuses submission without an email address, showing that the email box has been set as a required field.
